senses.sense_definition: To persuade, win over, or entice someone to do something through deception, cunning, or flattery.

examples.text: The salesman tried to <w>inveigle</w> the elderly woman into signing the costly contract.
She managed to <w>inveigle</w> her brother into doing all her weekend chores.

senses.sense_definition: To obtain or acquire something through clever manipulation, deceit, or cunning.

examples.text: Through sheer charm, he <w>inveigled</w> an invitation to the private dinner party.
The reporter managed to <w>inveigle</w> confidential information out of the director.

senses.sense_definition: To ensnare or entangle someone in an intricate or difficult situation.

examples.text: The young diplomat was quickly <w>inveigled</w> in the dangerous web of court intrigue.
Unwittingly, the investors found themselves <w>inveigled</w> in a complex fraudulent scheme.

traits.comment: Used in older literary texts to mean entrap or ensnare.

senses.sense_definition: To fool, delude, or impair the judgment of someone.

examples.text: False promises were crafted to <w>inveigle</w> the minds of the desperate citizens.
He feared that grand ambitions would <w>inveigle</w> his sense of justice.

traits.comment: Rarely used in modern English in this sense.
